title: Communion and the sending
hook: Catholics receive; others often come forward for a blessing; then go forth, the Mass is ended

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Agnus Dei, the Lamb of God, and the centurion's words. Your line was only say the word. Where did you let something good in? Day one hundred and seventeen.

Row by row, people stand and walk up the aisle in a slow line. An old woman with a walker. A dad carrying a sleeping toddler. A teenager in a hoodie. At the front, a priest or a lay minister holds up a small white host to each person and says four words: the Body of Christ. And each one answers with one word: Amen. Then something you might not expect. Mixed into the line are people who aren't receiving. They come up with their arms crossed over their chest, and the minister gives them a blessing instead. Nobody stares. Today, the last scene of the Mass, and the word for the whole thing.
screen: `ROW BY ROW, A SLOW LINE.` → `THE BODY OF CHRIST. AMEN.` → `ARMS CROSSED, FOR A BLESSING.`

segments.voice: Communion means union, sharing together. Catholics believe they receive Christ himself, so they prepare: at peace with God, having gone to confession for any serious sin, and fasting from food for an hour before. They receive on the tongue or in the hand, and sometimes from the cup too. That Amen is a whole creed in one word: yes, this is Christ, and yes, I belong to his body, the Church. Saint Augustine told new Christians something like: receive what you are, and become what you receive. Because communion is a sign of full unity in the Church, Catholics usually ask others not to receive. It isn't meant as a judgment on anyone. So in many parishes, anyone may come forward with arms crossed for a blessing. Afterward, there's silence. A last prayer. A blessing. And then the deacon or priest sends everyone out. In the old Latin: Ite, missa est. Go, it is the sending. That's where our word comes from. Missa became Mass. Christians have gathered for it every Sunday for nearly two thousand years, and for about sixteen hundred of them it has carried the name of its last line: you're being sent. It's the same root as mission. Look back over these two weeks. The entrance. Through my fault. Lord, have mercy. The Gloria. The readings, the Gospel and the homily. The creed and the prayers. The gifts carried up. Holy, holy, holy. The consecration. The Great Amen and the Our Father. The Lamb of God. And now, communion and the sending. The Mass doesn't end at the door. It's aimed at it.
screen: `COMMUNION: UNION, TOGETHER.` · `THE BODY OF CHRIST. AMEN.` · `A BLESSING FOR THOSE NOT RECEIVING.` · `ITE, MISSA EST: YOU'RE SENT.` · then: `FOURTEEN SCENES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan one kind thing after. Settle, and breathe. Picture walking out of wherever you are right now, out a door, into the rest of your day. Now ask: where am I being sent? Pick one person, and one kind thing you could do for them before tonight. A text. A favor. A patient answer. Be specific. If you pray, you can ask to be sent well. If not, just make it your mission for the day. The bell holds the time.
Mass. From the Latin missa, the sending: the whole Catholic liturgy, named for the moment the people are sent out. Today's word.
Your line: the Mass is a sending. That closes our walk through the Mass. Tomorrow, the rosary. Today, go and do the kind thing you picked. Day one hundred and seventeen.

howItsDone: Catholics who are prepared come forward to receive communion, answering Amen to 'the Body of Christ'; in many parishes those not receiving come forward with arms crossed for a blessing; after a closing prayer and blessing, the deacon or priest dismisses the people.

match.prompt: what's inside the end of Mass — tap the pairs.

myth: the word Mass comes from the moment of the sending
Ite, missa est: go, it is the sending. missa became Mass.
anyone at Mass is expected to receive communion
communion is a sign of full unity in the Church, so Catholics usually ask others not to receive. many come up for a blessing.
Catholics fast for a while before receiving
from food for an hour before communion.

fork.setup: you're visiting a Catholic Mass with a friend. you're not Catholic. the communion line reaches your row. what do many parishes invite you to do?
options: come forward with arms crossed for a blessing.
fork.reveal: many parishes invite anyone to come forward with arms crossed over the chest and receive a blessing. staying seated is fine too.

original.note: Latin: go, it is the sending (the dismissal). missa gave the whole liturgy its name.

trapdoor: what you thought: Mass is just the Catholic word for church.
what it means: the liturgy is named for its last line: the people receive communion, then are sent out.
what a scholar hears: missa, a late Latin form linked to mittere, to send, and to missio, mission. scholars still debate its exact first sense, dismissal or offering.

sources.ref: Catechism of the Catholic Church 1332, 1385–1398; Code of Canon Law 919 and 844

notes: The index hook says 'go forth, the Mass is ended' (ICEL wording). The script quotes only the Latin 'Ite, missa est' and translates it; confirm.
Preparation for communion (state of grace, confession for grave sin, one-hour fast, canon 919) summarized; confirm.

Non-Catholics and communion: the script says Catholics 'usually ask others not to receive'. Canon 844 allows exceptions (e.g. Orthodox Christians in some circumstances). The practice of coming forward for a blessing with arms crossed is widespread but not in the rubrics. A Keeper should confirm the wording is accurate and welcoming.
Augustine, Sermon 272 ('be what you see, and receive what you are'): paraphrased.
Etymology of missa: generally linked to the dismissal (mittere); the trapdoor notes debate. Confirm.
Part-two close (the Mass, days 104–117) recapped in the teach.

Audit (2026-09-30): the teach implied the liturgy has been called missa for two thousand years; the name is attested from the late fourth century (e.g. Ambrose). Reworded to 'for about sixteen hundred of them'. Keeper to confirm the dating.
